Consult Summary:
- Adult female developed progressive upper lip swelling and breathing difficulty ~30 minutes after eating prawn soup around 7 PM.
- Suspected anaphylaxis; ambulance arranged via 999; advised to take antihistamines while waiting and to follow up post-hospital for ongoing allergy management/injections.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Suspected acute allergic reaction/anaphylaxis after prawn soup.
- Timeline: Ate prawn soup ~7 PM; lip swelling began ~30 minutes later; swelling progressed and felt “pumping”/worsening.
- Symptoms: Upper lip swelling (left corner initially, then upper lip), difficulty breathing, dizziness; chest tightness uncertain; denies explicit throat closing but reports breathing difficulty.
- Pertinent history: Known peanut allergy since childhood; prior episode ~1 year ago after late-night curry with next-morning generalized swelling and breathing difficulty; childhood hospitalization for severe allergic reaction at ~age 6 per patient recollection; uncertain prior use of injection in childhood.
- Immediate management: Advised to take available antihistamines; instructed mother to call 999 for suspected anaphylaxis; ensure accompaniment until ambulance arrival; to seek hospital care urgently.

Issue 2:
- Asthma (pre-existing).
- Current therapy: Uses salbutamol inhaler; no other (brown) preventer inhaler reported.
- Relevance: Underlying airway disease with concurrent allergic reaction and dyspnea.

Issue 3:
- Peanut allergy.
- History: Since childhood; patient recalls hospitalization for severe reaction at ~age 6; sometimes uses antihistamines for this, agent unspecified.
- Possible additional allergen: Prawn/shellfish suspected based on current reaction (not confirmed).

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Antihistamines (unspecified, used sometimes for peanut allergy) — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- Peanut — longstanding; history of severe reaction requiring hospital care in childhood.
- Prawn/shellfish — suspected based on current episode; not formally diagnosed.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Severe allergic reaction in childhood requiring hospital care (per patient recollection).

Social History:
- Accompanied by mother at home during episode; living arrangements otherwise not documented.
- Alcohol: Not routinely documented; prior episode occurred after a night out with alcohol.

Preventative History:
- Not discussed/documented (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, BMD, vaccinations, optometry, skin check not recorded).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Examination findings: Not documented (teleconsult; patient-reported symptoms of lip swelling, dyspnea, dizziness).

Plan:
- Emergency care: Mother to call 999 for suspected anaphylaxis; patient to take available antihistamines while awaiting ambulance; remain accompanied.
- Post-hospital: Patient to contact clinic after discharge to arrange ongoing allergy management, including discussion of “injections” for severe allergic reactions and further planning.
- Safety: Advised urgent evaluation due to progressive symptoms and breathing difficulty.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Full medication reconciliation (names, doses, routes, frequencies), allergy verification and detailed reaction history, vitals and physical exam, comprehensive ROS, detailed asthma control assessment, smoking status, immunization/preventive care status.
- Internal conflicts: Patient reports difficulty breathing; chest tightness uncertain. Initially alone, then mother arrived during call (no clinical conflict).
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; some hesitations and incomplete sentences; clinically adequate information captured.
